analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that oil, gas, and mining companies disclose payments they make to governments.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the repeal 33-27 on party lines, but the full House never voted, and the bill died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Dodd-Frank required companies that extract oil, natural gas, or minerals to publicly report the payments — royalties, fees, and bonuses — they make to the U.S. or foreign governments. This bill deletes that requirement from the law. Investors and citizens would no longer be able to see how much a company paid a government for access to its resources.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and mining companies that would otherwise have to publish their payments to governments. They gain privacy over the sums they pay for drilling and mining rights, and avoid compliance costs. Investors who currently use this data also lose it.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 13(q) of the Securities Exchange Act, the provision requiring resource extraction companies to disclose payments to governments [S4].
Deletes Dodd-Frank Section 1504, the underlying disclosure mandate, including its conforming references [S4].
The Congressional Research Service describes the bill purely as a repeal of the payment-disclosure requirements for oil, natural gas, and minerals development [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Citizens of resource-rich countries lose a tool for tracking whether money their governments receive from extraction actually arrives; investors lose standardized country-by-country payment data; anti-corruption groups lose a transparency mechanism.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors and citizens seeking government-payment transparency

drawbacks.text: The repeal removes the public record of what companies pay governments for oil, gas, and mineral rights, eliminating one of the few tools for detecting misuse of resource revenue [S2] [S3] [S4].
It strips information from public securities filings, so investors in these companies lose standardized data on where and how much companies pay governments [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to companies is privacy over their payments and lower reporting compliance costs — the industry's long-stated objection to the rule. The cost is the loss of a transparency standard designed to let citizens and investors see the flow of money between extractive companies and governments, including in countries where corruption is a serious problem. The bill offers the public nothing in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it in a party-line 33-27 vote and placed it on the House calendar in January 2018, but no floor vote ever came, and the bill expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 1, 2017, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S6].
The committee marked it up on December 12-13, 2017, and ordered it reported by a vote of 33 to 27 [S6].
The committee reported the bill without amendment on January 9, 2018, as H. Rept. 115-500, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S3] [S6].
It never received a House floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and mining companies are better off: the disclosure requirement they opposed was never repealed, but no new obligation took effect either, and the bill's failure left the public-transparency fight unresolved while the companies avoided the compliance burden during that period.

for.name: Rep. Bill Huizenga
for.role: Sponsor; House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the resource extraction disclosure requirement

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to order the bill reported out of committee

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported, 33-27

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote split 33-27 along party lines, with Republicans voting to advance the repeal and Democrats opposed [S6].

industries.note: The bill spares them from publicly disclosing payments to governments for access to oil and gas resources, reducing public visibility into those dealings [S2] [S3]. The public benefit of that visibility is what the repeal removes.
Same mechanism for minerals: payments to governments would no longer have to be reported, shielding the company-government money flow from public view [S2] [S3].
These groups rely on government-payment disclosure to track resource revenue in corrupt-prone jurisdictions; repeal of the mandate eliminates their data source [S2] [S3].
